title: Chapter 73 — Buying Psychology: How Decisions Actually Happen
intro: Emotion and justification, loss aversion, and the reality that people are more afraid of buying the wrong refrigerator than they are of spending the money.

sections.title: People Buy Emotionally and Justify Logically
sections.content:
Every purchase decision starts with emotion and gets justified with logic. The customer falls in love with the French-door refrigerator because it looks beautiful in their kitchen. Then they justify it because it has the right capacity, fits the space, and the energy rating will save money.

Your job during the 10 Steps is to engage both systems. Discovery and wants assessment connect with the emotional side. Needs assessment and the complete ticket satisfy the logical side.

When you skip one side, the sale stalls. All logic and no emotion? The customer says 'it makes sense but I need to think about it.' All emotion and no logic? The customer says 'I love it but I can't justify it.'

sections.title: Loss Aversion Is More Powerful Than Gain
sections.content:
Behavioral science shows that people feel the pain of losing something roughly twice as strongly as the pleasure of gaining something of equal value.

In appliance sales, this means customers are more afraid of buying the wrong refrigerator than they are excited about buying the right one. They are not worried about missing a great deal — they are worried about making a mistake.

This changes how you close. Instead of selling the benefits, reduce the risk. Extended warranties reduce risk. Expert advice reduces risk. A thorough demo reduces risk. A strong return policy reduces risk. The reassurance stage after the close reduces risk.

Every part of your process should make saying yes feel safe.

sections.title: Decision Fatigue Is Real
sections.content:
A customer who has looked at 15 refrigerators is not more informed. They are more confused.

Too many options create decision fatigue — the point where the customer cannot choose because every option looks similar and they are afraid of picking wrong. The result is the worst outcome for everyone: no decision at all.

Your job during product recommendation is to narrow the field. Not to one option — that feels controlling. But to two or three well-chosen options that genuinely fit what you learned in discovery. Give them a clear choice between good options, not a wall of identical-looking products.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating psychological awareness, ask:

Does the salesperson engage both emotion and logic during the sale?
Do they reduce perceived risk throughout the process — or add to it?
Do they narrow options to prevent decision fatigue — or overwhelm the customer?
Do they understand that most hesitation is about fear of a bad decision, not about the money?
